1  Introduction

An autonomous agent inhabits a temporal world, observing a stream of high-dimensional sensory data from which it builds an internal model of how the world evolves. Learning latent dynamics from sequential observations is a natural path to such world models. An encoder compresses observations into a compact latent space, and a predictor captures temporal transitions, enabling planning and control without operating in the observation space. The Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) (LeCun, 2022) instantiates this idea. The JEPA objective alone, however, admits a trivial solution where the encoder maps everything to a constant. A popular fix today in modern self-supervised learning (SSL) is the stop-gradient trick, which passes the prediction target through the encoder but blocks gradients on that branch. This is used by many JEPA implementations (Assran et al., 2023; Bardes et al., 2024), and the closely related image SSL methods (Grill et al., 2020; Chen and He, 2021). Another alternative to stop-gradient is distributional regularizers (Zbontar et al., 2021; Bardes et al., 2022; Balestriero and LeCun, 2025). While the choice between the two is usually made for training stability, it also decides the structure of latent representations. A planner that searches in latent space (Zhou et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2026b, ; Maes et al., 2026) requires both geometry, where latent distance smoothly tracks progress toward the goal, and content, where task-relevant factors, such as an object to be manipulated, stay decodable.

We find that many common choices lead to poor geometry. With stop-gradient (SG), the target is held fixed during each update, so the encoder is trained only to predict its current latents. This one-sided objective does not ask consecutive latents to lie on a smooth path. In our experiments, a smooth route often appears jagged in the SG latent. Latent distance then becomes a poor guide toward far goals, and SG falls behind on hard maze goals. The one-sided objective is also fragile when data are scarce. In contrast to SG, common distributional regularizers fall short in a different way. VICReg and SIGReg were designed for i.i.d. multi-view batches and constrain the whole latent distribution.

In contrast, a regularizer with fewer constraints yields a better latent map. In this paper, we introduce sliced variance regularization (SVReg), a one-sided floor on the spread of the latent along random directions, trained without SG. The target then moves with the encoder, so the whole latent is trained to be predictable from its past, and directions the predictor cannot explain, such as noise, are suppressed. In our experiments, a smooth route then stays smooth in the latent. The resulting latent is a smooth map of the agent’s state. Its distances track progress in navigation and reaching, and in first-person mazes its leading principal components trace the agent’s position.

However, the predictability pressure can erase task-relevant content. Factors are penalized for their unpredictable variance, so slow, hard-to-predict factors, such as manipulated objects, can be lost. In comparison, SG variants tend to keep these factors, but at the cost of the jagged geometry described above. Together, the two failures form what we call the content–geometry tradeoff.

To achieve the best of both worlds, we propose Slow SVReg. It adds 1) a slowness term, which encourages a small portion of the latent to change slowly across frames, and 2) a gated residual predictor, which copies the current latent by default and predicts the change. Both favor slowly changing factors. Slow SVReg keeps these factors in manipulation and improves planning, especially in first-person mazes, where the agent’s position must be carried across frames. Slow SVReg plans best on hard maze goals, Reacher, Cube and PushT. Moreover, a model trained on Wanderland city walk scans (Liu et al., 2026) learns a latent map of the streets from first-person video and actions.

Our contributions are as follows. First, we show that SG and common distributional regularizers learn poor latent geometry for planning, while SVReg learns smooth latent maps in navigation and reaching. Second, we identify the content–geometry tradeoff, analyze its direction in the linear encoder objective, show how modes compete for latent capacity in controlled experiments on latent linear dynamics, and find the same pattern in visual control. Finally, we introduce the slowness regularizer and the gated residual predictor, which favor slowly changing factors and keep content more reliably. The resulting model performs strongly across navigation, mapping, reaching, and manipulation.

2  Analysis

This section explains where the content–geometry tradeoff comes from and motivates our main method in Section 3, through the lens of linear latent dynamics. Without stop-gradient, the encoder is penalized for unpredictable variance (Section 2.1). This suppresses noise, but it also shrinks hard-to-predict factors, which can then be dropped when the latent has too few dimensions to hold every factor (Section 2.3). With stop-gradient, finite data can lead the encoder to read noise while its latent statistics look healthy (Section 2.2).

We analyze TT observations with a linear encoder Φ​(𝒐)=W​𝒐\Phi(\symbfit{o})=W\symbfit{o} and an action-conditioned linear predictor 𝒛^t+1=A​𝒛t+B​𝒂t\hat{\symbfit{z}}_{t+1}=A\symbfit{z}_{t}+B\symbfit{a}_{t}, where 𝒛t=Φ​(𝒐t)\symbfit{z}_{t}=\Phi(\symbfit{o}_{t}). The JEPA loss (LeCun, 2022) is

This loss admits a trivial collapse in which Φ\Phi maps every observation to the same constant (Φ≡0\Phi\equiv 0 for the linear encoder). The remedies are a stop-gradient on the target (Assran et al., 2023; Bardes et al., 2024), or a regularizer on the latent distribution (Zbontar et al., 2021; Bardes et al., 2022; Balestriero and LeCun, 2025; Kuang et al., 2026).

Removing unpredictable directions, including observation noise, therefore reduces the loss and can give a smoothly moving state a smooth latent path. 2.2  Finite Data

Finite-sample noise has a nonzero lag-1 cross-covariance, of order σ2​d/T\sigma^{2}\sqrt{d/T} for observation dimension d≪Td\ll T and noise level σ\sigma. When this spurious lag structure exceeds the signal’s, the fixed-target objective can select it, and the encoder keeps healthy latent variance while reading noise instead of state. We call this failure signal collapse. In-sample statistics cannot detect it, since the selected noise directions mimic signal lag correlations and a variance regularizer rescales them to meet its floor. A held-out state probe does detect it (Proposition A.1 in Section A.4).

2.3  Content

While good geometry captures latent dynamics, task-relevant content such as the state of a manipulated object can still be lost. Consider one scalar component of the environment state that evolves as st+1=φ​st+κ​at+ϵts_{t+1}=\varphi s_{t}+\kappa a_{t}+\epsilon_{t}. Its persistence φ\varphi measures how much of it carries over to the next step, so a mode with φ\varphi near 11 changes slowly. Its one-step residual δ\delta is the share of its variance that is not predicted by the current state and action. Without stop-gradient, a less predictable mode adds more prediction loss, and SVReg shrinks its latent coordinate.

The variance floor keeps the mode’s scale away from zero, so shrinkage alone keeps the mode readable (Section A.5). Content is lost when modes compete for too few latent dimensions. We analyze this competition in the linear case, where two modes share one coordinate (Proposition A.2 in Section A.5). For persistent modes, with or without stop-gradient, a new mode enters the latent more easily when it is more persistent than the mode already there. Without stop-gradient, it also enters more easily when the action explains more of its variance, and the cost of one coordinate carrying two dynamics can protect the incumbent, so whichever factor fills the latent first can keep it. A manipulated object rests most of the time and moves only through contact, so the action explains little of its variance, and the latent can trade it for an action-driven factor such as the arm. SVReg loses the cube’s height early in training, as this competition predicts (Figure 5b). In Appendix B we also test the competition of capacity with a linear experiment (Figure 7).

3  Learning Geometry and Content

In this section, we introduce Slow SVReg. It trains without stop-gradient with sliced variance regularization (SVReg) for geometry, and adds slow channels and a gated residual predictor to favor slowly changing factors (Figure 2). We also define measures of content and geometry. The baselines are described in Section 5.1.

Sliced variance regularization.

VICReg and SIGReg (Section 5.1) were designed for i.i.d. multi-view batches and constrain the whole latent distribution, toward decorrelated coordinates or an isotropic Gaussian. World model data are temporally correlated trajectories whose states need not follow such a distribution, even with ample data, which motivates a less restrictive regularizer. Sliced variance regularization (SVReg) puts a one-sided floor on the standard deviation of the latent along random directions:

ℛSVReg(z)=𝔼𝒖[max(0, 1−stdt(𝒛t⋅𝒖))2],𝒖∼Unif(𝕊r−1),\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{SVReg}}(z)=\mathbb{E}_{\symbfit{u}}\!\left[\max\!\left(0,\,1-\mathrm{std}_{t}(\symbfit{z}_{t}\cdot\symbfit{u})\right)^{2}\right],\qquad\symbfit{u}\sim\operatorname{Unif}(\mathbb{S}^{r-1}), (1)

where 𝒛t⋅𝒖\symbfit{z}_{t}\cdot\symbfit{u} projects each latent onto the direction 𝒖\symbfit{u} and stdt\mathrm{std}_{t} is taken over the estimation sample. The squared hinge is active only when the standard deviation along the direction falls below 11. Restricting 𝒖\symbfit{u} to the coordinate axes gives the element-wise floor, a squared form of the variance term of VICReg (Bardes et al., 2022). A latent can satisfy the element-wise floor while two coordinates copy each other, leaving no variance along their difference. SVReg also checks such mixed directions, without requiring the coordinates to be decorrelated. We add SVReg with weight λ\lambda to the JEPA prediction loss without stop-gradient, just like VICReg and SIGReg.

Slow channels.

SVReg alone can lose content that rarely changes and moves only through contact, such as a resting cube. We therefore train a small fixed set of latent channels to change slowly between frames. For the slow channels 𝒃t\symbfit{b}_{t}, we add the slowness term with weight β\beta,

ℛslow​(𝒃)=𝔼t​‖𝒃t+1−𝒃t‖22​tr​Var​(𝒃).\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{slow}}(\symbfit{b})=\frac{\mathbb{E}_{t}\|\symbfit{b}_{t+1}-\symbfit{b}_{t}\|^{2}}{2\,\mathrm{tr}\,\mathrm{Var}(\symbfit{b})}. (2)

This is a variance-normalized form of the slowness objective of slow feature analysis (Wiskott and Sejnowski, 2002), so shrinking the slow channels cannot reduce the term, while SVReg covers the whole latent. It resembles the invariance term of VICReg applied to consecutive frames, but acts on a subset of channels and is normalized by their variance. Prior world models apply slowness along trajectories to the whole latent, in JEPA objectives such as PLDM (Sobal et al., 2025; Hauri et al., 2026) and as a regularizer that keeps consecutive latents close (Xia et al., 2026). The closest split designs constrain a fixed part of a representation (Garrido et al., 2023b, ; Denton and Birodkar, 2017).

Gated residual predictor.

The gated residual predictor is a second way to favor slow factors. It copies the current latent by default and learns the change, so a factor that does not change between frames costs nothing to predict. The linear dynamics of Section 2.3 already have this form, st+1=st+((φ−1)​st+κ​at)+ϵts_{t+1}=s_{t}+\bigl((\varphi-1)s_{t}+\kappa a_{t}\bigr)+\epsilon_{t}. For a persistent mode, φ\varphi near 11 makes the change without action small, as for a resting object or the agent’s position between moves. We use

𝒛^t+1=𝒛t+𝒄⊙f​(𝒛≤t,𝒂t),\hat{\symbfit{z}}_{t+1}=\symbfit{z}_{t}+\symbfit{c}\odot f(\symbfit{z}_{\leq t},\symbfit{a}_{t}), (3)

where 𝒂t\symbfit{a}_{t} is the action and 𝒄\symbfit{c} is a learned per-dimension gate initialized at c0=0.1c_{0}=0.1. This has the same form as LayerScale (Touvron et al., 2021), which scales residual branches across depth, whereas this gate scales the predicted change over time.

The identity path makes slowly changing factors cheap to predict, while the slow channels add direct pressure toward slow change. Together, they are designed to favor slow factors without SG, echoing SG’s local preference among competing modes. We call this model Slow SVReg.

Measuring content and geometry.

We measure both properties on held-out data, separately from planning success. Content is the held-out R2R^{2} of ridge readouts of state factors (agent position, joint angles, cube position and height, block pose), fit and scored on separate episodes, and the area under the ROC curve for binary factors such as gripper–cube contact (0.50.5 is chance). We measure two aspects of geometry, the ordering of latent distances and the smoothness of latent paths. The distance rank correlation ρ\rho is the Spearman correlation between latent distance ‖𝒛−𝒛′‖\|\symbfit{z}-\symbfit{z}^{\prime}\| and true task distance (shortest path in PointMaze, joint space in Reacher). In manipulation, cost-to-goal ρ\rho correlates the latent L2 distance between two held-out frames (the planner’s cost) with their true state distance (Appendix C). Jaggedness encodes a scripted smooth motion, such as a maze route or a full Reacher shoulder turn, and compares path lengths before and after a short moving average 𝒛¯t\bar{\symbfit{z}}_{t},

J=∑t‖𝒛t+1−𝒛t‖∑t‖𝒛¯t+1−𝒛¯t‖,J=\frac{\sum_{t}\|\symbfit{z}_{t+1}-\symbfit{z}_{t}\|}{\sum_{t}\|\bar{\symbfit{z}}_{t+1}-\bar{\symbfit{z}}_{t}\|}, (4)

4  Noisy Linear Dynamics

We first test the geometry prediction of Section 2 in a linear world whose map is known. A two-dimensional state rotates at frequency ω\omega and is observed through a random orthonormal map U∈ℝ32×2U\in\mathbb{R}^{32\times 2} with Gaussian noise,

𝒔t+1=Rω​𝒔t,𝒐t=U​𝒔t+σ​𝒏t,𝒏t∼𝒩​(0,I),\symbfit{s}_{t+1}=R_{\omega}\,\symbfit{s}_{t},\qquad\symbfit{o}_{t}=U\symbfit{s}_{t}+\sigma\symbfit{n}_{t},\quad\symbfit{n}_{t}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I),

where RωR_{\omega} is the rotation by angle ω\omega and σ=0.3\sigma=0.3 (protocol in Appendix B). The circle is an easy task, since a PCA of the raw observations can recover the latent easily. The experiment is therefore a unit test that asks whether a JEPA objective can also find a latent linear map.

Interestingly, SG fails most at fast frequencies and short trajectories, as shown in Figure 3. By comparison, SVReg stays near the signal-recovery ceiling up to ω≈1\omega\approx 1, and SG + SVReg lies between them. Slow SVReg matches SVReg on slow signals. With its default small gate (c0=0.1c_{0}{=}0.1) it loses the fastest signals (above ω=0.5\omega=0.5 at T=250T{=}250), and a gate of c0=1c_{0}{=}1 keeps them up to ω≈1\omega\approx 1. In Figure 3, we show the different learned latent maps. Each encoder maps a loop, as an agent walking a closed route would. Without SG the map is a ring ordered by phase, while SG encodes scattered points without circular geometry.

The dependence on trajectory length follows the finite-data argument of Section 2.2. The spurious lag structure of the noise shrinks as σ2​d/T\sigma^{2}\sqrt{d/T}, so a frozen-target encoder can select noise directions on short trajectories and needs longer ones to recover the circle. Without stop-gradient, SVReg penalizes unexplained target variance and so removes the noise directions at every length. The analysis does not predict the dependence on frequency, which we report as an empirical finding.

A second linear experiment tests content under limited capacity (Appendix B). An action-driven arm and an object that moves only when the arm touches it compete for a latent smaller than their joint state. SVReg keeps the arm with the best geometry but drops the object in about half the seeds (Figure 7). SG keeps the object at the cost of arm geometry, and SG + SVReg lies between them.

5  Visual Control

In this section, we test whether geometry and content decide planning success in visual goal-reaching with an action-conditioned JEPA. In navigation and reaching the agent moves only itself, and in manipulation it also moves an object.

5.1  Setup

Environments. We evaluate PointMaze U-maze and Medium (Fu et al., 2020), Reacher-Hard (Tassa et al., 2018), OGBench-Cube (Park et al., 2025) and PushT (Chi et al., 2025). Top-down PointMaze and Reacher train on one uniform-random exploration trajectory, first-person PointMaze on one trajectory of smooth random driving, Cube on 2,000 scripted-expert episodes and PushT on DINO-WM’s offline dataset (Zhou et al., 2025).

Models and baselines. All models trained from scratch share a task-specific ResNet encoder and an action-conditioned transformer predictor (architectural details in Section C.2). VICReg (Bardes et al., 2022) combines element-wise variance and covariance penalties. As in other JEPA world models, it is paired with action-conditioned next-latent prediction, so on temporal data it has no term that keeps consecutive latents close. SIGReg, the sketched isotropic Gaussian regularizer (Balestriero and LeCun, 2025), matches Gaussianity along random slices. As in LeWM (Maes et al., 2026), we apply SIGReg after a BatchNorm MLP projector on the encoder output and call this SIGReg-BN. The projector is the only difference from plain SIGReg, and the other objectives act on the encoder output directly. LeWM computes the SIGReg statistics per frame, while LeJEPA pools them over the batch. To give SIGReg-BN its best chance, we ran both forms on every task and use the one that plans better (Appendix C). Per-frame statistics plan better on Cube, Reacher and the first-person mazes, and statistics pooled over the batch and time on the top-down mazes and PushT. Two hybrids test whether explicit regularization yields geometry with SG. SG + SVReg adds SVReg (Equation 1), and SG + straightening adds the temporal-straightening curvature penalty (Wang et al., 2026b, )

ℛcurv​(z)=1T−2​∑t=0T−3(1−cos⁡(𝒛t+1−𝒛t,𝒛t+2−𝒛t+1))\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{curv}}(z)=\frac{1}{T-2}\sum_{t=0}^{T-3}\Bigl(1-\cos\bigl(\symbfit{z}_{t+1}-\symbfit{z}_{t},\;\symbfit{z}_{t+2}-\symbfit{z}_{t+1}\bigr)\Bigr) (6)

over a training window of length TT, which is 0 along a straight latent path.

Planning and selection. Cross-entropy method (CEM) model-predictive control minimizes latent distance from predicted states to the goal image and replans after a few steps, as in DINO-WM (Zhou et al., 2025). In the mazes, easy goals lie 25 steps from the start with no filter on their distance, and hard goals lie 50 steps away and at least 3 maze units apart. Cube is scored on all goals and on the goals that move the cube by at least 4 cm (≥\geq4 cm, about 60% of goals). For each method, task and goal set we select one encoder learning rate and regularization weight, the setting with the highest mean success on a separate planning seed over all training seeds. We report that setting on three other planning seeds (Appendix C). Unless stated otherwise, tables report the mean and standard deviation over six training seeds at the selected setting. Bold marks the best value and underline the second best.

5.2  Main Results

Slow SVReg plans best on hard maze goals from both views, on Reacher, on both Cube protocols and on PushT (Tables 1 and 2). In the mazes, easy goals nearly saturate for the strongest methods, while hard goals lie 50 steps away along long routes and test whether latent distance tracks progress toward the goal. SVReg alone shows where the two properties matter. It plans second only to Slow SVReg on hard goals in navigation and reaching, where only the agent moves, but it falls behind SIGReg-BN on Cube and SG + SVReg on PushT, with widely varying success. We trace its strength in navigation to geometry (Section 5.3) and its weakness with objects to lost content (Section 5.4).

In Table 2, we report planning in first-person view mazes, and the gaps widen. Here, the agent sees only the view ahead, so its position must be inferred from the views and actions. On hard goals SG drops sharply and the other baselines stay well below SVReg, while Slow SVReg nearly saturates on both mazes. Among the agent-only tasks, its gain over SVReg is largest here and small in the top-down mazes and Reacher, where each frame shows the agent.

SG + SVReg and SG + straightening add a geometry term to SG. They plan better than SG on hard U-maze goals and on PushT, but trail SVReg on hard Medium goals in both views and on first-person U-maze.

5.3  Geometry

Figure 4 plots the top two principal components of held-out latents in both mazes, colored by the agent’s position. Without SG, SVReg and Slow SVReg show the maze layout in the PCA plot. Nearby positions are close in the representation space, and the corridors of Medium appear as separate branches. The layout emerges from first-person views as well, where the agent never sees its true position. SG keeps only a coarse ordering by position from above, and with first-person views its latents, like those of SG + straightening, mix positions from across the maze. The SVReg paths are smooth as well. A smooth shortest route stays smooth in most SVReg latents and zigzags under SG (Appendix D), and a full turn of the Reacher shoulder traces a smooth closed loop under SVReg and a jagged one under SG.

A latent map can be right globally and still be hard to plan with. The planner reaches a far goal by following latent distance over many short replanning steps, so it depends on the local shape of the latent and not only on its global layout. We therefore compare planning with two measures of geometry: the jaggedness of latent paths, a local measure, and the rank correlation between latent distance and maze distance over all frame pairs, a global measure. Jaggedness tracks planning closely. On U-maze, Medium and Reacher, the three methods with the most jagged paths are also the three weakest planners (Tables 7 and 8). The rank correlation does not track planning. SG + SVReg plans hard U-maze goals well although its latent distance barely follows the maze. Planning success follows path smoothness more closely than global distance ranking, which fits a planner that compares latent distances over a few steps.

5.4  Content

Geometry alone does not explain the object tasks. On Cube, SIGReg-BN and SG + straightening plan second and third in Table 1 although their latent distances follow goal distance least well, while SVReg ranks goal distance well and still plans poorly. Here the planners differ in content, and in particular in the cube rather than the arm (Table 9). VICReg, SVReg and SG + SVReg, the weakest Cube planners, detect gripper–cube contact least reliably, and SVReg can lose the cube’s height (Figure 5b).

PushT shows the same effect more sharply. A resting block changes only when the agent pushes it, so it is hard to predict from the agent’s motion. VICReg, SIGReg-BN and SVReg all lose it, and their held-out block readouts fall below predicting the mean (Table 10). The two best PushT planners in Table 1, Slow SVReg and SG + SVReg, both keep the block.

Keeping this content usually costs geometry. Along single knobs on Cube, such as predictor depth or the slowness weight, a higher cube-height readout comes with a lower body ρ\rho (Figure 5a). Slow SVReg reaches the high-content end of this tradeoff and gives up little geometry. It reliably keeps cube height and contact, keeps the PushT block in most runs (Figure 1b), and its cost-to-goal ρ\rho stays close to SVReg’s on both tasks. Two-stage, an SVReg head trained on a frozen SG encoder, keeps content but plans below Slow SVReg on all tasks (Appendix D).

5.5  Content Is Decided Early

The random initial encoder decides which SVReg runs lose cube height. For each training seed, the three objectives start from the same encoder, and SVReg fails exactly from the initial encoders that read the least height. From these starts, SG keeps acquiring height while SVReg does not (Figure 5b). In shorter reruns, Slow SVReg acquires height from all starts, more slowly from the weakest ones (Figure 5b).

Once acquired, height survives the removal of SG. In Appendix F, switching from SG to SVReg at 20k steps keeps cube height and plans better than SG. SVReg’s content failure therefore lies in acquisition.

5.6  Ablation

Table 4 adds the slow channels and the gated residual predictor (GR) to SVReg separately and together, and Table 4 adds GR to the other objectives on Cube. Each part fixes a different failure of SVReg, and together they give the largest gains on Cube and PushT. On Cube, the slow channels alone give most of the gain, while the gated residual alone fails in some runs, even over a larger set of training runs, where Slow SVReg never does. In these runs the latent stays longer in an early phase of fast, jittery change and acquires cube height late. The two failing runs we continued recover with twice the training steps, so their failure is a delay beyond the step budget. On PushT, both parts raise success, but the block becomes readable mainly with the gated residual (Appendix E).

We find that these gains are tied to the sliced floor trained without SG. Restricting SVReg’s directions to the coordinate axes gives the element-wise floor, which loses cube height and plans at about 50% on Cube (Appendix E). Under SG, the predictor’s default copy is a trivial solution, and SG with the gated residual collapses to a latent without cube information (Table 4). Without SG, the gated residual also raises VICReg’s Cube success.

5.7  Data Scaling

We test whether the gains hold beyond the dataset sizes and training budget adopted in Table 1. In Figure 13, Slow SVReg reaches high success from little data. On hard U-maze goals it nearly saturates with a fifth of the Table 1 data, where SG stays far below even with all of it. On Medium and Reacher, it plans well above SVReg and SG with only 1k to 2k frames, and on Cube it plans better than both from 5k frames up to the Table 1 size (protocol in Appendix G).

In Figure 11, Slow SVReg on PushT improves with longer training. With a short learning-rate cooldown, its success keeps rising up to 150k steps. SG + straightening, the next-best method, improves at a similar rate, and Slow SVReg keeps its lead.

6  City Walks

Inspired by the results in first-person mazes, we next ask whether the same recipe learns a map from first-person video and actions of real places. Wanderland (Liu et al., 2026) provides 3D Gaussian-splat reconstructions (Kerbl et al., 2023) of real city blocks and buildings, captured on foot. In each scene we render first-person walks with random turns and forward steps along the capture path, and train on the frames and actions only, without poses (Appendix H). Linear readouts fit on the training walks give the agent’s position and heading on held-out walks. A map score measures how well the top two principal components of the latent lay out the walked area, and a held-out disc outside the training walks tests how far the map extends.

In Table 5, linear readouts of the latent recover position for the objectives trained without SG. Slow SVReg reads position most accurately on scene 13Skv and remains the most accurate in the held-out area, where every readout extrapolates. SG also reads position, and it reads heading better than the SVReg variants. SG + straightening reads position in some runs and loses it in others, and among the trained models VICReg has the largest position errors. An untrained encoder of the same architecture reads position barely better than predicting the mean position and keeps no map.

The latents trained without SG also recognize places across viewing directions. For most validation frames, the nearest training frame in the latent among those facing more than 90∘90^{\circ} away was taken within 5 m, whereas SG mostly matches views with similar headings (Appendix H).

What Slow SVReg and SVReg add is geometry. In Figure 6, the walked layout appears in the leading principal components of their latents, with no fitted readout. Slow SVReg forms the clearest map, followed by SVReg, both well above the other single-stage objectives (Table 5).

The map forms with experience. In Figure 14, position error drops by an order of magnitude as the training walks grow from two to one hundred and revisit the same streets. Earlier predictive and slow-feature models found position codes in simulated or small real environments, mostly through trained decoders (Section 7). Here the street layout of a reconstructed city block appears in the plain principal components of an action-conditioned JEPA trained without poses or stop-gradient.

We also train separate models on ten further scenes, four indoor and six outdoor, at the scene-13Skv setting, with two runs per scene. In Table 12, an SVReg variant has the highest map score in all ten scenes, most often Slow SVReg. Using a linear readout, SIGReg-BN localizes best across scenes, but its leading components form no map.

7  Related Work

Self-supervised learning and anti-collapse.

To prevent collapse, contrastive methods use negative pairs (Chen et al., 2020; He et al., 2020), and non-contrastive methods with stop-gradient, with or without an exponential moving average (EMA) target (Grill et al., 2020; Chen and He, 2021), or centering (Caron et al., 2021). These objectives are equivalent under limited assumptions (Garrido et al., 2023a, ). Barlow Twins decorrelates (Zbontar et al., 2021), VICReg floors element-wise standard deviations (Bardes et al., 2022), and SIGReg and VISReg match a Gaussian shape along random slices (Balestriero and LeCun, 2025; Wu et al., 2026). BYOL also trains with weight-standardized group normalization instead of batch normalization (Richemond et al., 2020). Theory shows that the non-contrastive objective collapses without stop-gradient (Tian et al., 2021) and characterizes the features it learns (Tang et al., 2023; Littwin et al., 2024). Our floor is one-sided like VICReg’s and sliced like SIGReg’s, and we compare a stop-gradient target with a regularized target that receives gradients by what content and geometry each keeps for a planner.

JEPA and world models.

JEPA learns through temporal prediction (LeCun, 2022) and scales to images and video (Assran et al., 2023; Bardes et al., 2024). Latent dynamics support planning in World Models, PlaNet, Dreamer, TD-MPC and DINO-WM (Ha and Schmidhuber, 2018; Hafner et al., 2019, 2020, 2021; Hansen et al., 2022, 2024; Zhou et al., 2025). PLDM trains without SG using VICReg-style losses, inverse dynamics and whole-latent slowness (Sobal et al., 2025), and LeWM uses SIGReg from pixels (Maes et al., 2026). Terver et al., (2025) study what drives planning success in JEPA world models, and AdaJEPA adapts a pretrained JEPA world model at test time under SG (Wang et al., 2026a, ). Content loss also appears in JEPAs that focus on slow features and fail with a fixed distractor (Sobal et al., 2022), and in Pong, where LeWM suppresses the ball that a stop-gradient variant recovers (Karmann et al., 2026). We analyze how the target gradient affects content and noise, and favor slowly changing content without SG.

Temporal representation learning and straightening.

Slow Feature Analysis extracts slow features under unit-variance and decorrelation constraints (Wiskott and Sejnowski, 2002), CPC contrasts future observations with unrelated ones (van den Oord et al., 2018), and deep networks have used the temporal coherence of video frames to learn image features (Mobahi et al., 2009; Goroshin et al., 2015; Jayaraman and Grauman, 2016). Koopman methods learn linear latent dynamics, scored by VAMP (Wu and Noé, 2020) or trained with autoencoders (Lusch et al., 2018), and JEPA connects to Koopman invariant subspaces (Ruiz-Morales et al., 2025). Perception straightens natural-video trajectories (Hénaff et al., 2019), and explicit curvature regularization supports latent planning (Wang et al., 2026b, ). Our no-stop-gradient objective is VAMP-like in the linear setting (Theorem 2.1), but SVReg learns smooth latent paths with nonlinear encoders and predictors, without a curvature penalty.

Spatial representations from prediction.

Predictive and slow-feature models encode position, but prior work reads it mostly through trained decoders or single units. Examples are navigation agents with auxiliary tasks (Mirowski et al., 2017, 2018), world models with belief states or next-frame prediction (Gregor et al., 2019; Gornet and Thomson, 2024), and slow feature analysis of camera views in small areas (Franzius et al., 2007; Metka et al., 2018). Without a decoder, coarser structure appears in the top principal components of a network that predicts 20-dimensional sensor readings (Recanatesi et al., 2021) and in spatially contiguous k-means clusters of a regularized world model (Xia et al., 2026). In our latents, the top two principal components lay out first-person mazes and the walked streets of reconstructed city blocks, learned from frames and actions without poses.

8  Conclusion

A latent world model for planning needs to learn content that encodes task-relevant states, and geometry that smoothly tracks progress toward a goal. SG, whose target is one-sided, learns content but poor geometry, and common regularizers, which constrain the latent feature distribution beyond a variance floor, also struggle with geometry. In contrast, SVReg learns smooth latent maps, but it can lose task-relevant content. To address this tradeoff, we introduce Slow SVReg, which favors slowly changing factors. It keeps this content and improves planning. Slow SVReg plans best in the hard settings of visual control tasks, and moreover, in first-person mazes and city walks, it also learns the map layout in its leading principal components.

Part (1) of Theorem 2.1 restates known VAMP and Koopman results (Mardt et al., 2018; Wu and Noé, 2020; Ruiz-Morales et al., 2025). Earlier analyses follow each mode separately. Under stop-gradient, joint updates of encoder and predictor generally do not follow the gradient of a scalar objective (Ponce et al., 2026), so Part (2) of Theorem 2.1 describes a single update against a frozen target. Appendix C Experimental Setup Details

C.1  Data and Baselines

Data.

PointMaze U-maze (5k frames), PointMaze Medium (20k frames) and Reacher (5k frames) are each trained on one exploration trajectory with uniform-random actions. Cube is trained on 2,000 episodes of the OGBench scripted expert (80k frames). PushT uses the offline dataset of DINO-WM (Zhou et al., 2025). In first-person PointMaze, the agent drives a unicycle through the maze and sees only the corridor in front of it. Its data come from one exploration trajectory of smooth random driving, with 5k frames on the U-maze and 20k on Medium, and the encoder and planner follow the top-down setup.

Baselines.

VICReg applies its variance and covariance terms to all frames of the batch. The straightening penalty skips near-stationary steps and averages over the remaining ones. Two-stage selects its SG trunk and head learning rates by the selection rule of the other methods.

PushT uses the final predicted step for the early CEM iterations and this weighted cost afterwards, and Cube uses the final predicted state only. Sampled actions are clamped to [−1,1][-1,1] on the mazes and Reacher. On PushT, unbounded CEM drives the agent out of the arena, so actions are clamped to the data’s action range, ±4\pm 4 in normalized units or about the 0.1–99.9th percentiles. The Cube planner is unbounded, and OGBench clips Cube actions to [−1,1][-1,1]. Bounding it lowers SG and SVReg by a few points and keeps their order.

Goals.

In PointMaze, easy goals are 25 steps from the start with no filter on how far they lie, and hard goals are 50 steps away and at least 3 maze units apart. Cube goals are 25 environment steps ahead with a 50-step budget, as in LeWM (Maes et al., 2026). The Cube all column scores all goals, and the ≥\geq4 cm column scores only goals whose cube moves more than 4 cm (about 60% of goals). Our start and goal frames come from held-out episodes, whereas LeWM draws them from its training episodes.

Scoring.

Planning success is the percentage of episodes that reach the goal within the step budget (0 to 100, higher is better). Each trained model is scored by its mean success over three planning seeds, with 50 episodes each or 100 on Reacher. The plan column of the geometry tables in Appendix D reports success at the Table 1 setting, on hard goals in PointMaze.

C.4  Hyperparameter Selection

Grids.

Encoder learning rates range over {10−6,10−5,10−4,5×10−4,10−3}\{10^{-6},10^{-5},10^{-4},5{\times}10^{-4},10^{-3}\}. Regularization weights range from 0.3 to 1000 for SVReg and Slow SVReg, 1 to 300 for SG + SVReg, 0.01 to 100 for VICReg and 10−410^{-4} to 1000 for SG + straightening. SIGReg-BN uses 0.3 to 30 with pooled statistics and 0.05 to 192 with per-frame statistics. For two-stage, the SG trunk is trained with learning rate 10−610^{-6} or 10−510^{-5}, and the SVReg head with learning rate 10−410^{-4}, 5×10−45{\times}10^{-4} or 10−310^{-3}. The head’s SVReg weight is 1 on Cube and 10 on the other tasks.

Selection rule.

Settings are selected on a separate planning seed. Grids are trained on three training seeds, and the leading settings on three more. For each method and task we take the setting with the highest mean success over all six, breaking ties by the lower learning rate and then the smaller weight. Each column is selected on its own goals, so the easy, hard, all and ≥\geq4 cm columns can use different settings.

SIGReg-BN.

SIGReg-BN screens its grid on one training seed and trains its two best settings per task on the rest. The per-frame grid multiplies the pooled setting’s weight by 1/64, 1/16, 1/4, 1 and 4 at three learning rates around the pooled setting’s, and extends an axis while the best setting lies on its edge. With pooled statistics, PushT uses encoder learning rate 10−510^{-5} only. The statistic form omitted from Table 1 plans worse on all tasks.

First-person PointMaze.

Each method is selected from its learning-rate grid as in Table 1. SIGReg-BN (both statistic forms), VICReg and SG + SVReg also screen the weight grids of their top-down maze runs and extend their best settings before selection.

C.5  Metrics

Readouts (content).

Readout R2R^{2}, AUC, distance rank correlation, jaggedness and the participation ratio (eff. dim) are defined in Section 3. Readouts are ridge regressions (α=1\alpha{=}1) fit on one set of held-out episodes and scored on another, with 18 and 7 episodes on Cube and 15 and 6 on PushT.

  • •

    Cube. Contact AUC detects gripper–cube contact with a linear readout. Free cube R2R^{2} reads the cube position on frames without contact and with the gripper at least 5 cm away, and grasped arm R2R^{2} reads the gripper position on contact frames. The cube-height R2R^{2} in Figure 5b also comes from a linear readout.

  • •

    PushT. Agent R2R^{2} reads the agent position. Free block R2R^{2} reads the block position and angle (xx, yy, cos⁡θ\cos\theta, sin⁡θ\sin\theta) on frames where the block does not move and the agent is at least 60 px away, and pushed block R2R^{2} reads them on frames where the block moves.

Distance correlations (geometry).

Higher is better for all measures below, and rank correlations range from −1-1 to 11.

  • •

    Reacher. Dist. ρ\rho is the Spearman correlation of latent and joint-space distance. 10-NN is the overlap of the 10 nearest neighbors of a frame in latent and joint space (0 to 1).

  • •

    PointMaze. Geodesic ρ\rho is the Spearman correlation between the latent L2 distance of two held-out frames and the shortest-path distance between their agent positions inside the maze. It uses 150 anchors ×\times 1,500 frames from the second half of the held-out trajectory. Local ρ\rho restricts it to pairs at most one maze cell apart.

  • •

    Cube and PushT. Cost-to-goal ρ\rho is the Spearman correlation, over 20,000 random pairs of held-out frames, between the latent L2 distance (the planner’s cost) and the true state distance. The true state is the gripper and cube positions in meters on Cube (all 25 held-out episodes). On PushT, it is the agent and block positions in pixels plus the block-angle difference scaled by 20/(π/9)20/(\pi/9) px/rad, over all 21 held-out episodes. This scaling gives the angle tolerance of the success check, π/9\pi/9, the weight of its position tolerance, 20 px.

Jaggedness.

Jaggedness uses a 9-step moving average over the full latent. In PointMaze it is the mean over five smooth shortest routes, a fixed route and four routes between random cell pairs at least half as long. The routes are rendered in the simulator at zero velocity, with first-person views facing the direction of travel. The Reacher sweep turns the shoulder through 360∘360^{\circ} at elbow 60∘60^{\circ}. Cube has no scripted motion, so its jaggedness is the mean over each held-out episode’s frames before the first gripper–cube contact, over 25 segments with at least 20 frames and 2 cm of arm travel each. The true state path on these segments has jaggedness 1.09.

Appendix D Latent Geometry and Content

PCA panels show the top two principal components of held-out frames from the Table 1 checkpoints, and the tables use the full latent.

PointMaze.

Table 7 gives the path and distance measures of the maze latents in Figure 4 and Figure 8.

Reacher.

A Reacher frame shows two joint angles. The shoulder turns fully and the elbow covers ±160∘\pm 160^{\circ}, so a faithful latent is a smooth surface with one loop for the shoulder. The elbow may close a second loop, because the two fully folded poses look alike. We pose the arm in the simulator, turn the shoulder through 360∘360^{\circ} at a fixed elbow and project the frames onto each method’s PCA. In Table 8, SVReg and SG + SVReg trace one smooth closed loop, while SG and two-stage trace jagged paths. As in the mazes, local smoothness tracks planning more closely than the global ranking of distances.

Cube.

The Cube state space has two sheets that meet at grasp and release. Without contact, arm and cube move independently, and the latent must keep the cube’s position although nothing moves it. During a grasp, the cube moves with the gripper, so the latent should be a smooth function of the arm. Table 9 gives ridge readouts on held-out episodes for the free cube, contact and geometry, and Figure 9 shows the latent PCA of all methods in Reacher and Cube. SIGReg-BN and VICReg keep cube height only in low-variance components. VICReg and SVReg are the only methods that fail to separate contact in some runs. SVReg merges the two sheets in three of six runs, which are also the runs that lose cube height.

PushT.

The PushT state is the agent position and the block pose. In Table 10, SVReg’s block readout does not transfer to new episodes in five of six runs, whether the block rests or is pushed, and its leading principal components carry the agent instead. Figure 11 traces content and geometry along single knobs on the full PushT dataset.

Two-stage.

Two-stage freezes an SG encoder and trains a fresh head, predictor and action encoder on its output with SVReg and without SG (Table 6). Table 11 compares it with SG and Slow SVReg on all tasks.

Appendix E Content and Ablation Details

Content.

At the Table 1 settings, Slow SVReg reads cube height (R2≥0.98R^{2}\geq 0.98) and separates contact in every run, and keeps the PushT block in five of six.

Ablation.

The gated residual alone fails, with Cube success below 80% on all goals, in three of the six runs of Table 4 (λ=30\lambda=30). Over 16 training seeds at λ=10\lambda=10, the gated residual alone fails in four and Slow SVReg in none. On PushT, the resting-block R2R^{2} is 0.12, 0.59 and 0.79 with slow channels, the gated residual and both.

Early phase.

We rerun four seeds of each variant at λ=10\lambda=10 with intermediate checkpoints and measure jitter as the variance-weighted share of latent power at periods under five model steps on held-out trajectories. At step 5000, the gated residual alone is jittery in three seeds and reads height less well (R2R^{2} 0.54–0.79), while Slow SVReg is already smooth (R2R^{2} 0.99). The two failing seeds recover by 100k steps (89% and 87%). The slow channels hold almost none of the height readout’s weight, and slowness on the whole latent without a slow block also removes all failures over the 16 seeds.

Controls.

The element-wise floor plans at about 50% on Cube and reads cube height poorly (R2<0.5R^{2}<0.5) at every λ∈{1,10,100}\lambda\in\{1,10,100\}. SG with the gated residual reads no cube height in any run.

Appendix H City Walks

Data.

The random walker stays within 1.2 m of the capture path, where renders stay sharp, and moves into nearby geometry are refused using the rendered depth. The main scene, 13Skv, has 100 training walks of 500 steps, 10 validation walks and a set of held-out walks. A disc of radius one seventh of the walkable extent is held out of all training walks and is scored as a separate set.

Models.

The encoder, predictor and objectives follow the maze setup. SIGReg-BN uses per-frame statistics in City Walks, as in LeWM. The untrained control has random weights and BatchNorm statistics recalibrated on the training walks (three initializations). Predicting the mean position gives a 28.0 m error.

Selection.

We select each method’s learning rate and regularization weight by the lowest validation position error on one training seed. Table 5 averages the selected setting over three further runs, and Figure 6 shows the best of them. The ten further scenes use two runs each.

Other variants.

With pooled statistics, SIGReg-BN localizes less accurately and forms no map on any of the eleven scenes. On 13Skv, two-stage (Appendix D, one setting) maps nearly as clearly as Slow SVReg but reads position less accurately, and SG + straightening reads position in two of three runs.

Metrics.

Position and heading come from ridge readouts fit on 6,000 training-walk frames and scored on the validation walks and the held-out disc. The map score is the Procrustes R2R^{2} between the top two principal components of the validation latents and the true positions: 1 for a rotated and scaled copy of the walked area, 0 for no layout. For cross-heading recall (Section 6), chance is 4% and the untrained encoder reaches 5%. On scene 13Skv, Slow SVReg, SIGReg-BN and SVReg reach 75–89%, VICReg and two-stage 26–36%, and SG + straightening and SG about 10%. The ten further scenes give a similar ranking.
